result.summary: Telemachus and Minerva (as Mentor) reach Pylos, where Nestor feasts them and tells of the Greeks' troubled returns from Troy and the murder of Agamemnon. Minerva vanishes as an eagle, Nestor sacrifices a heifer to her, and Telemachus leaves by chariot with Pisistratus for Lacedaemon.

scenes.title: Arrival and feast at Pylos
scenes.summary: Telemachus, encouraged by Minerva, joins the Pylian sacrifice to Neptune and asks Nestor for news of Ulysses.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus risks failing to learn his father's fate and must overcome his shyness before an elder.

scenes.title: Nestor tells of the returns
scenes.summary: Nestor recounts the quarrel of the Atreidae, the scattering of the fleet, and the fates of returning heroes, urging Telemachus to emulate Orestes.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans face the anger of Minerva and Jove on their voyages home.

scenes.title: Agamemnon's murder explained
scenes.summary: Telemachus laments the suitors; Nestor explains how Aegisthus seduced Clytemnestra and killed Agamemnon.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus's household and life are threatened by the suitors; Agamemnon lost his life through betrayal.

scenes.title: Menelaus's wanderings; advice
scenes.summary: Nestor tells of Menelaus's storm-tossed return, Orestes' revenge, and advises Telemachus to visit Menelaus.
scenes.stakes: Menelaus lost ships and a steersman in storms; Telemachus's estate is in danger while he is away.

scenes.title: Minerva departs as an eagle
scenes.summary: Minerva urges libations, declines Nestor's hospitality, and flies off as an eagle; Nestor prays to her and lodges Telemachus.

scenes.title: Sacrifice of the heifer
scenes.summary: At dawn Nestor and his sons sacrifice a gilded heifer to Minerva, and Polycaste bathes Telemachus.

scenes.title: Chariot journey to Pherae
scenes.summary: Telemachus and Pisistratus ride off and spend the night with Diocles at Pherae, then continue.

notable_quotes.reason: Pisistratus voices the Homeric view that all people need the gods.
Orestes is held up as the model avenging son.
Even gods cannot save a man whose hour has come.

analysis.text: Telemachus comes of age as he is urged to match Orestes and gains confidence through Minerva's guidance.
The feast, sacrifice and guest-friendship show the central role of ritual hospitality (xenia) in Homeric society.

legacy.text: The Orestes–Aegisthus story told here is the model later dramatized by Aeschylus in the Oresteia.

fun_facts.text: Nestor's tale of the returns (nostoi) draws on a lost epic tradition, the Nostoi, about the Greeks' voyages home.

language_notes.text: Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is called lord of the Earthquake because he was thought to shake the earth; he was the chief god of Pylos.
"Inward meats" are the entrails, such as heart, liver and lungs, which were roasted and eaten first at a sacrifice.
Minerva is disguised as Mentor, an Ithacan friend of Ulysses, so Telemachus addresses her by that name.
"Vouchsafe" means to condescend or graciously agree to grant something.
A hecatomb was originally a sacrifice of a hundred oxen, later any large sacrifice.
"Knight of Gerene" is Nestor's standing epithet; "knight" here means a charioteer or horseman from Gerene, a place associated with him.
The question was conventional: pirates were not despised in this world, and a host could ask whether guests were traders or raiders.
Amphitrite is the sea goddess, wife of Neptune; her name stands here for the sea itself.
Privateering means raiding for plunder; here it refers to the Achaeans' sea raids on coastal towns during the Trojan War years.
"Peer of gods in counsel" means equal to the gods in wisdom; it is a stock compliment for Patroclus.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) was angered because the Achaeans had not honored her at Troy, notably through Ajax the Less's outrage at her shrine.
Hecatombs were large sacrifices of cattle, originally a hundred oxen, offered to win a god's favor.
"Bandying hard words" means trading angry insults back and forth.
Agamemnon was murdered on his return home by Aegisthus, his wife Clytemnestra's lover; Orestes later avenged him.
"Show your mettle" means prove your courage and character.
"Honour to the Achaean name" means Nestor brings glory to the Greeks; Achaeans is Homer's common term for the Greeks generally.
"Heaven has a long arm" means the gods' power reaches far, so they can save a man even from a great distance.
Telemachus addresses Minerva as "Mentor" because she has disguised herself as Mentor, an old friend of Ulysses; he does not know she is a goddess.
"Elsewhither" is an archaic word meaning to some other place.
A "barrow" is a burial mound; Nestor says Aegisthus would have been denied a proper grave.
"Cajoled" means persuaded by coaxing or flattery.
"Batten upon" means feed greedily on.
"Painless shafts" means arrows that bring a gentle, sudden death; Apollo was thought to cause such deaths.
"Counselled evil against him" means Jove planned harm for him; "waves ran mountains high" is a vivid way of saying the waves were enormous.
"Gathered much gold and substance" means he collected wealth and goods, probably through trade or gifts, among foreigners.
"Bane" means destroyer, the cause of someone's ruin or death.
"Out of his reckoning" means far off his intended course; "twelve-month" means a year.
"Order the tongues of the victims to be cut": the tongues were cut out and burnt as a final offering to the gods before the company slept.
Water was poured over the hands for ritual washing; the mixing-bowls held wine blended with water, as the Greeks normally drank it.
The Cauconians were a people of the region south of Pylos. Minerva's story of a debt is a pretext, since she is a goddess in disguise.
"Trito-born" is an epithet of Minerva (the Greek Athena), of uncertain origin, linked to a river or lake called Triton.
"Vouchsafe" means to graciously grant or condescend to give.
"Aegis-bearing" refers to Jove's aegis, a divine shield or goatskin cape that inspires terror, which his daughter also carries.
"Child of morning" and "rosy-fingered" are Homer's fixed way of naming dawn, repeated whenever a new day begins.
"Guardian of the public weal" means protector of the community's welfare; Nestor rules and judges as king of Pylos.
"Propitiate" means to win the favor of a god by offering sacrifice.
Gilding a heifer's horns was a mark of costly sacrifice, meant to please the goddess with beauty.
The women's "screaming with delight" is a ritual cry (ololyge) raised at the moment of the killing, not a cry of fear.
Thigh bones wrapped in fat were the gods' share, burned for them. The people then ate the rest of the meat.
"Inward meats" are the entrails, such as the heart and liver, eaten first by the worshippers.
"Nothing loth" means not unwilling; the horses ran eagerly.

context_notes.text: Pylos was Nestor's kingdom in the western Peloponnese. Nestor, son of Neleus, was the oldest and wisest Greek leader at Troy.
Pisistratus is Nestor's youngest son and becomes Telemachus' companion on the rest of his journey.
Ulysses had not returned from Troy, and Telemachus is searching for news of him.
Nestor, aged king of Pylos, fought at Troy and is the wise elder; Telemachus has come to ask him for news of Ulysses.
The son of Tydeus is Diomed, a leading Achaean warrior at Troy.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is god of the sea, so sailors thanked him for safe passage.
Orestes, son of Agamemnon, killed his father's murderer Aegisthus. He is repeatedly held up as a model for Telemachus.
Nestor, king of Pylos, is very old and famed for wisdom, and he fought at Troy.
Aegisthus was Agamemnon's cousin. He took over Argos and Agamemnon's wife while Agamemnon was away at Troy.
Sunium is the southeastern tip of Attica, the territory of Athens, and had a famous temple on its headland.
Aegisthus seduced Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra and murdered Agamemnon on his return. His son Orestes later avenged him, a story often held up as a model for Telemachus.
Lacedaemon is Sparta, the kingdom of Menelaus.
Minerva is disguised as Mentor, an older man, and has been accompanying Telemachus on his search for news of his father Ulysses.
Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, fought beside Ulysses at Troy. Hospitality to guests was a strong sacred duty.
Lacedaemon is Sparta, where Menelaus lives. Telemachus will go there next to ask for news of Ulysses.
Gilding a sacrificial animal's horns was a lavish honor to a god, and the unyoked heifer was considered pure.
Neleus was Nestor's father and the former king of Pylos. "House of Hades" means the underworld, realm of the dead.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is present unseen to accept the offering; earlier she had visited Pylos in the form of Mentor.
Pherae was a town on the road from Pylos toward Sparta, where Telemachus is heading to seek news of Ulysses.

literary_notes.text: The sunrise over the sea opens the scene with a formal epic setting of time and light.
Telemachus shows his youth and shyness, a contrast to the confident speaker he will become.
The goddess is pleased at being given precedence, which shows that Pisistratus has unknowingly honored a god.
The phrase 'every man's hand against you' recalls a proverbial image of an outlaw at odds with everyone.
Telemachus ends by invoking his father's past service, a rhetorical plea based on reciprocal obligation.
Nestor's question stresses how vast the Achaeans' suffering was, beyond any human telling.
Nestor's rambling aside about Telemachus resembling his father shows him as talkative, warm and quick to praise.
Nestor comments with the hindsight of an old man, judging Agamemnon's folly and stating a general moral about the gods.
Orestes is offered as a model son whose action contrasts with Telemachus's passive situation, setting up the urging to act.
Nestor's recollection of Minerva's open favour for Ulysses reveals his habit of reminiscing and underlines the goddess's special protection of the hero.
Minerva's mention of a murder at home foreshadows Ulysses' own dangerous homecoming and contrasts it with Agamemnon's fate.
Telemachus despairs of his father's return while the disguised Minerva stands beside him and the audience knows Ulysses is alive.
"False Aegisthus" fixes his treachery as his defining trait, in the manner of Homeric epithets.
The aside about Phrontis's skill makes his sudden death more poignant and shows the narrator's admiration for him.
Orestes' funeral banquet and Menelaus's arrival coincide, so Menelaus returns to a house already avenged and misses the crime's reckoning.
Saying even birds cannot cross the distance in a year stresses how far Menelaus was driven.
The eagle, a bird associated with Jove and with omens, reveals the divine presence and marks her favor toward Telemachus.
Nestor's quick inference shows him as wise and pious, and he reads the sign as proof of Telemachus' future greatness.
Nestor turns to address the departed goddess directly, as though she were still present, in a prayer of gratitude.
The repeated "rosy-fingered Dawn" is a formulaic epithet that marks time and gives the poem its ritual rhythm.
He "looked like a god" after bathing, showing how hospitality and care transform Telemachus and raise his standing.
Swaying yokes and falling darkness convey the long day's journey in compressed, physical detail.
The repeated dawn and "nothing loth" horses echo the earlier lines, a recurring pattern of departure and travel.
